summary: The measured orientation dependence in YBCO bicrystals supports the importance of biaxial texture addressed by Goyal’s textured-substrate method. This is support for the design rationale, not a replication of tape performance or proof of a direct historical derivation.
The TFMC’s implemented NINT winding-pack technology enabled the reported high-field magnet test in that apparatus; this relationship does not assert that every NINT magnet reaches 20.1 T.
The internal demountable pancake-to-pancake joints provided low-resistance current transfer between modules of the implemented TFMC stack-in-plate assembly.
The intentional 31.5 kA open-circuit quench tested passive self-protection in the fusion-scale NINT TFMC and produced localized thermal damage in this non-optimized design.

The reported 20.1 T TFMC demonstration supports representative-scale magnet readiness for the authors’ high-field REBCO fusion pathway. This is component-level support; it does not establish plasma gain or net electricity generation.

Molodyk’s tested high-field industrial YBCO wire supports materials feasibility for high-field REBCO fusion-magnet designs: the TFMC program specifically cites industrial tape performance and volume as enabling large-scale magnets. No supplier-lot identity for every TFMC tape is inferred.
